glosses: A cheerful attitude; happiness; a good, happy, or positive mood.

examples.text: I have not that alacrity of spirit, / Nor cheer of mind, that I was wont to have.

glosses: That which promotes good spirits or cheerfulness, especially food and entertainment prepared for a festive occasion.

examples.text: a table loaded with good cheer

"And am I to meet my Mary at Moffat? Come away, little, dear, welcome body, thou blessed of heaven, come away, and taste of an auld shepherd's best cheer, and I'll gang foot for foot with you to Moffat, and my auld wife shall gang foot for foot with us too. I tell you, little, blessed, and welcome crile, come along with me."

“[…]the awfully hearty sort of Christmas cards that people do send to other people that they don't know at all well. You know. The kind that have mottoes like
 Here's rattling good luck and roaring good cheer, / With lashings of food and great hogsheads of beer.[…].”

glosses: A cry expressing joy, approval or support, such as \"hurrah\".

examples.text: Three cheers for the birthday boy!
A cheer rose from the crowd.
Welcome her, thunders of fort and of fleet! / Welcome her, thundering cheer of the street!

glosses: A chant made in support of a team at a sports event.
One's facial expression or countenance.

examples.text: And soo on the morne they were alle accorded that they shold departe eueryche from other / And on the morne they departed with wepynge chere / and euery knyȝt took the way that hym lyked best
examples.translation: And so they all agreed that they should depart from each other in the morning / And in the morning they departed with weeping faces / and every knight took the way that pleased him best
examples.english: And so they all agreed that they should depart from each other in the morning / And in the morning they departed with weeping faces / and every knight took the way that pleased him best

examples.text: Heraclitus taking pitie and compassion of the very same condition of ours, was continually seene with a sad, mournfull, and heavie cheere [translating visage], and with teares trickling downe his blubbered eyes.
‘thorough evill rest of this last night, / Or ill apayd or much dismayd ye be; / That by your change of cheare is easie for to see.’

glosses: One's attitude, mood.

examples.text: The parents […] fled away with heavy cheer.
And anon he talked with them, and sayde unto them: be of good chere, it is I, be not afrayed.

glosses: To gladden; to make cheerful; often with up.

examples.text: We were cheered by the offer of a cup of tea.

⁠How often shall her old fireside
⁠Be cheer’d with tidings of the bride,
How often she herself return, […]

glosses: To infuse life, courage, animation, or hope, into; to inspirit; to solace or comfort.

examples.text: The proud he tam'd, the penitent he cheer'd.

glosses: To encourage to do something.

examples.text:
Let’s cheere our ſouldiers to incounter him, […]
And burne him in the fury of that flame,
That none can quench but blood and Empery.

glosses: To applaud or encourage with cheers or shouts.

examples.text: The crowd cheered in support of the athletes.
The crowd cheered the athletes.

glosses: To feel or express enthusiasm for (something).

examples.text: The finance sector will cheer this decision.

glosses: Cheerleading, especially when practiced as a competitive sport.

examples.text: Alex participated in cheer all four years of college.
I'm going to wear my new cheer shoes at cheer today.
...[P]erspective [sic] gym cheer programs must address how to support a cheer program while maintaining appropriate and safe skill progressions.

2000, Linda Villarosa. Cheerleading Changes, and Injuries Increase in The New York Times.
Last year, more than 75,000 high school participants took part in cheerleading competitions, and the National Federation of State High School Associations says that "competitive cheer" is the fastest growing sport for girls.

2018, Chad Thompson. Iowa Central cheer team is tops at national competition in The Messenger.
The Iowa Central Community College cheer team has achieved something no other college in Iowa has before.

glosses: Balls or pieces of ice falling as precipitation, often in connection with a thunderstorm.
An occurrence of this type of precipitation; a hailstorm.
A rapid, intense barrage by a large number of projectiles or other objects.

examples.text: Their lack of good intelligence also meant that they vastly overestimated the size of their foes for far too long, hails of armor-piercing shells doing comparatively little damage compared to the high explosive that they should have been using.

glosses: To have hailstones fall from the sky.

examples.text: They say it's going to hail tomorrow.

glosses: To send or release hail.

examples.text: The cloud would hail down furiously within a few minutes.

glosses: To pour down in rapid succession.
Healthy, whole, safe.
To greet; give salutation to; salute.

examples.text: […] Farewel happy Fields / Where Joy for ever dwells: Hail horrours, hail / Infernal world, and thou profoundeſt Hell / Receive they new Poſſeſſor: […]

glosses: To name; to designate; to call.

examples.text: Such a Son as all men hail'd me happy;
He was hailed as a hero.

glosses: To call out loudly in order to gain the attention of.

examples.text: Hail a taxi.
'Cause I've got one hand in my pocket / And the other one is hailin' a taxi cab

glosses: To call out loudly in order to gain the attention of.
To indicate, from a designated stop or otherwise, to the driver of a public transport vehicle that one wishes to board and travel on the vehicle, usually using hand signals such as waving.

examples.text: In Melbourne, you would usually have to hail a tram when you are travelling late at night and there are no other passengers waiting at your stop.

glosses: To signal in order to initiate communication with.
In the game of uppies and downies, to throw (the ball) repeatedly up and down at the goal location, in order to score a point.
to originate (from), be native (to) or be based (in)
An exclamation of respectful or reverent salutation, or, occasionally, of familiar greeting.

examples.text: Hail, brave friend.
